extracted.intended_audience: natural philosophers, chymists, and physicians (early-modern/chemical practitioners and educated readers)
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and criticisms for how chymists identify, name, and demonstrate 'principles' (salt, sulphur, mercury) and other products of fire/distillation; focuses on what experimental proof and qualities suffice to claim elemental simplicity or composition. Aimed at guiding critical assessment of chymical experiments and nomenclature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle/element must be perfectly homogeneous
rubrics_metrics.description: An Element or Principle ought to be perfectly Similar and Homogeneous; nothing that is further resoluble into distinct substances deserves the name of a true Principle or Element.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not call a production of the fire a Principle (salt, sulphur, mercury) unless it is shown to be homogeneous and not further resoluble; similarity in some qualities is insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement of ocular/experimental demonstration of simplicity
rubrics_metrics.description: Chymists must convincingly and manifestly show by experiment (ocular proof) that the substances they call Salt, Sulphur, or Mercury are truly simple and homogeneous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rhetorical assertion or naming by resemblance is not enough; experiments must demonstrate simplicity rather than mere affinity in outward appearance or quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Naming by predominancy only justified when demonstrably predominant
rubrics_metrics.description: It is weak to name a substance after a Principle on the ground that that Principle is predominant, unless there is demonstrable evidence that the pure Principle exists and predominates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors should not rely on the custom of naming by a predominant quality without first showing that Nature produces pure instances of the named Principle and that it truly predominates in the specimen.

rubrics_metrics.name: Qualitative signs (taste, smell, volatility, inflammability, fixity) are unreliable as sole criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Qualities commonly used to identify chymical principles—taste, smell, volatility, inflammability, fixity, fusibility—can be shared by very different bodies and thus do not by themselves establish elemental identity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid inferring elemental composition from single sensory or simple experimental traits; compare multiple lines of evidence and be cautious about generalizing from such signs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Must account for production-method dependence (fire, distillation, closed vessels)
rubrics_metrics.description: Products obtained by the action of fire (distillation, incineration) can be new kinds of mixts and will vary with the method (e.g., closed vessel distillation vs open incineration) and degree of heat.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating results, require clear specification and control of experimental conditions (vessel sealing, amount/intensity of fire) because outcomes (fixed salts, volatile salts, oils) depend on them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish volatile salts from fixed (alcali) salts and avoid conflation
rubrics_metrics.description: Volatile (easily driven off) salts and fixed alkali salts differ markedly in properties (fixity under fire, taste, smell, medicinal virtues) and should not be treated as identical elementary substances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classifications and medical attributions must respect observed disparities (e.g., behaviour under heat, crystal forms, medicinal efficacy) rather than lumping all 'salts' together.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extracts/tinctures obtained by spirit of wine are not necessarily pure sulphurs
rubrics_metrics.description: Tinctures or extracts obtained by spirit of wine often constitute magisteries or mixtures of multiple ingredients rather than pure Chymical Sulphurs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not call a tincture 'sulphur' merely because spirit of wine dissolves it; analyze whether the extract contains saline, mercurial, or other ingredients and recognize it may be a compound extract.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimental evidence must show sameness across preparations before generalizing
rubrics_metrics.description: Apparent resemblances (colour, odour, behaviour) across products from different concretes do not prove identity; one must demonstrate sameness across preparations and sources before asserting a shared elementary nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seek reproducibility and cross-source consistency (e.g., same crystal forms, same resolvability) before treating diverse products as the same Principle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware terminological license—use names to reflect composition, not mere resemblance
rubrics_metrics.description: Chymists often license the abuse of words by naming substances after resemblances; authors should resist this and apply names that reflect actual composition and demonstrable properties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor precise nomenclature indicating mixture or uncertain composition rather than prematurely assigning elemental labels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of reaction behaviour and mutual affinities as diagnostic evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Observations of interactions (e.g., ebullition/hissing when mixing acids and ashes; precipitation colours; differing crystal shapes) are important indicators of disparity among supposed 'same' salts or principles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include and weigh reaction-behaviour evidence (mutual antipathy, precipitation, colour changes) when assessing claims of sameness or elemental identity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not generalize from destructive preparations (incineration) to natural elementary composition
rubrics_metrics.description: Many salts and substances are only obtained after violent incineration; such products may be fire-generated and not reflective of the natural, pre-existing elemental constitution of the concrete.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between products that are artifacts of the method (fire-produced) and those genuinely pre-existing in the substance; avoid concluding that incineration products reveal innate elementary composition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Require careful discrimination of multiple coexisting products from one concrete
rubrics_metrics.description: A single concrete may yield multiple distinct salts/oils/tinctures (sometimes with opposite properties); thus one must not assume a single underlying Principle for that concrete.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design experiments and analyses to separate and characterize each coexisting product (volatile salt, fixed salt, sal_armoniiack, oyl, tincture) instead of collapsing them into one category.
